measurement.happened:
PROTESTS AND STRIKES DOMINATE THE WEEK. This is by far the biggest story. France has experienced at least four consecutive weekends of mass demonstrations, with the largest turnout reaching 575,000 to 600,000 people on November 5-6, making it the biggest day of protest in years. The movement started as youth-led and student protests over education and cost of living, then expanded when trade unions joined forces for nationwide strikes on November 5. SNCF expected disrupted traffic with one TGV in ten cancelled. The demands center on higher wages, a 'dignified wage,' education funding, and student demands. Police clashed with protesters in Paris, Lyon, and other cities. A petrol bomb was thrown at police, triggering an 'attempted murder' probe. A police officer's home was destroyed by fire, per the interior minister. The Yellow Vests urged 'mass disobedience.' The PM, Lecornu, brought forward a minimum wage hike and announced a social conference as a response. Students blocked access to a Paris high school. The WSJ noted the riots were fueled by an 'ultra left' faction that lives off-the-grid. The movement spread across Europe, with Gen Z mobilizing in France, Albania, and India. A petition to ban a TV channel accused of stirring anti-immigration sentiment gained traction. Posts whipped up anti-Muslim sentiment as France reeled from street violence. The budget was unanimously rejected by parliament, deepening the fiscal impasse. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5, 7, 9; AP Nov 1, 2, 5, 7; AFP Nov 1, 2, 5, 7; BBC Nov 5; CNN Nov 5, 6; DW Nov 1, 2, 5, 6, 7; TV5Monde Nov 1, 5, 7; Bloomberg Nov 5; WSJ Nov 5; FT Nov 5; CNBC Nov 5, 8; Al Jazeera Nov 5, 6, 7, 8.)

CYBERATTACKS AND THE IRAN BLAME. France officially blamed Iran for an 'unprecedented' cyberattack on supermarket refrigerators across Europe, a story that broke on November 9. French blood banks were also hit, though no blood products were compromised. Credit Mutuel Arkea reported 100 million euros missing after a cyberattack. France vowed retaliation. The US also suspected Iran was behind the fridge hacking. This is a significant escalation in France's cybersecurity posture. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5, 6, 9; AP Nov 9; BBC Nov 4, 9; CNN Nov 9; DW Nov 4, 9; WSJ Nov 9; FT Nov 9; Bloomberg Nov 4; Al Jazeera Nov 9.)

2027 PRESIDENTIAL RACE INTENSIFIES. Polls show Le Pen and Mélenchon ahead in the 2027 race. Judo champion Teddy Riner announced a presidential run, pledging to 'bring people together' and described as a 'blank page' by the French public. Mélenchon pledged economic stimulus and renewed his call to exit NATO, calling for a 'revolutionary' remaking of society. Macron proposed a 'coalition' from Lisnard to Glucksmann before the presidential, without great success. Bardella accused Mélenchon of 'promoting the replacement' of France's 'historical people.' Le Pen said 'there is no discrimination' in France. Glucksmann criticized Macron's coalition as 'discrediting politics.' Philippe highlighted his 'differences' with Macron. RSF laid out ten priorities for 'the right to information' for the 2027 race. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 7, 9; AP Nov 7, 9; AFP Nov 9; TV5Monde Nov 6, 7, 9; FT Nov 7; Al Jazeera Nov 7.)

G7 TALKS IN PARIS. G7 foreign ministers met in Paris to discuss Iran, Ukraine, and AI, with a conciliatory tone amid multiple crises. Secretary of State Rubio traveled to Paris for his first post-midterm foreign trip, facing questions on Trump policies after the US midterm setback. The G7 ministerial location was switched at the last minute amid the protest movement. Allies assessed the impact of Trump's midterm loss. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5, 6, 9; AP Nov 6, 9; AFP Nov 9; TV5Monde Nov 9.)

RUGBY NATIONS CHAMPIONSHIP. France crushed Fiji 54-17 but lost fly-half Ntamack to a hamstring injury, a major blow ahead of the decisive match against South Africa at Twickenham. The Dupont-Ntamack partnership's return was noted 600 days after their last pairing. Galthie lamented the loss. Veterans were recalled due to injuries. Dupont called the Nations Championship a 'World Cup rehearsal.' (Supported by: Reuters Nov 7; AP Nov 6, 7; AFP Nov 5, 7, 8; TV5Monde Nov 5, 6.)

ECONOMIC PRESSURE. Fitch downgraded France's outlook in a surprise update. Rising debt costs threaten economic stability. The Bank of France is likely to cut its 2026 GDP forecast. The budget was unanimously rejected by parliament. Air France-KLM beat profit forecasts but KLM flagged further cost cuts. SocGen will cut about 40 branches by 2027. France raised the cap on the popular Livret A savings account in February. France urged the EU to adopt a higher fast fashion levy. Trump's Cuba swing puts French and Chinese firms in crosshairs. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 3, 5; DW Nov 8; Bloomberg Nov 3, 5; FT Nov 5; CNBC Nov 5; TV5Monde Nov 5.)

DEFENSE AND MILITARY. France will protect a NATO hub in Poland from January. France ordered a long-range naval cruise missile from MBDA. France extended its maritime patrol plane's stay in the Black Sea after cargo ship attacks. The EU and France launched a scheme linking French firms with Ukrainian defence startups. Europeans will join Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi. A covert Russian network exploited French riots on social media, per an EU report. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 5, 6, 9; AP Nov 8; TV5Monde; FT Nov 4.)

SPORTS AND CULTURE. Alcaraz won the Paris Masters, beating Shelton in the final, taking revenge after a previous loss. Djokovic and Zverev crashed out early. Mbappé headlines Zidane's France football squad, with a surprise call-up for striker Pagis. PSG set a Champions League record as the fastest side to score four goals. Disney and Skydance are eyeing TV rights bids for Ligue 1. The Goncourt prize went to Philippe Jaenada. Over 200 authors denounced sexism in French literary prizes. Céline Dion went on with her concert in Paris despite protests. The New Yorker covers were displayed in France. A Bartholdi exhibition opened at the Bourse de Commerce. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 3, 6, 7, 8, 9; AP Nov 3, 6, 7, 8; AFP Nov 3, 4, 5; BBC Nov 3, 4, 7, 8; TV5Monde Nov 3, 6, 9; FT Nov 9; Bloomberg Nov 9; WSJ Nov 4.)

HEALTH AND PUBLIC SAFETY. Avian flu risk was raised to 'moderate' in France. A bus carrying schoolchildren crashed in eastern France, killing two and injuring 16. A doping ban was handed to Paris Olympics weightlifting medalist Andreev. (Supported by: Reuters Nov 6; AP Nov 6; AFP Nov 6; TV5Monde Nov 4; BBC Nov 6.)

delta.motion:
The most dramatic change between the two photographs is the acceleration of the protest movement. In the first image, the third weekend drew 320,000 to 400,000 people, mostly youth and students, with clashes concentrated in Paris. By the second image, the fourth weekend on November 5-6 pulled 575,000 to 600,000 people into the streets, the largest turnout in years, and the movement had widened to include trade unions calling nationwide strikes, with SNCF cancelling one TGV in ten. The violence escalated: a petrol bomb was thrown at police, a police officer's home was set on fire, and the Yellow Vests entered the fray urging mass disobedience. The government's response shifted from deploying 70,000 police to bringing forward a minimum wage hike and promising a social conference, a more substantive concession than the small gestures of the first week. The budget, which was already under pressure in the first photograph, was unanimously rejected by parliament in the second, deepening the fiscal impasse.

The Trappes shooting, a prominent and emotionally charged story in the first photograph, largely vanished from the headlines by the second. The suspect was under psychiatric observation, and the case faded into the background noise of the broader political argument, no longer generating its own news cycle. The NFL game in Paris, the Olympics leadership change, the BHV Marais bankruptcy, and the dockers' strike all shrank or disappeared from the top of the news, replaced by larger stories.

What appeared and grew fastest were three themes. First, the cyberattack story exploded from a minor note about supermarket refrigerators in the first photograph to a full diplomatic and financial crisis in the second: France officially blamed Iran, blood banks were hit, Credit Mutuel Arkea reported 100 million euros missing, and France vowed retaliation. Second, the 2027 presidential race widened and intensified. Teddy Riner, the judo champion, announced a presidential run, Mélenchon called for exiting NATO, Macron proposed a broad centrist coalition, and Bardella clashed publicly with Mélenchon. The field is more crowded and more chaotic than a week earlier. Third, defense and military developments grew: France committed to protecting a NATO hub in Poland, ordered a long-range naval cruise missile from MBDA, extended its Black Sea patrol, and the EU launched a scheme linking French firms with Ukrainian defence startups. A covert Russian network exploiting the riots on social media was also reported.

The G7 foreign ministers' meeting in Paris, with Secretary of State Rubio visiting for his first post-midterm foreign trip, appeared entirely as a new story in the second photograph. Sports and culture continued but shifted: the focus moved from the NFL and Olympics to the Rugby Nations Championship (France crushed Fiji 54-17 but lost Ntamack to injury), Alcaraz winning the Paris Masters, and Mbappé headlining Zidane's squad. Health and public safety stories, including an avian flu risk upgrade and a school bus crash killing two children, appeared for the first time.
delta.wind:
The expectation of a fourth weekend of mass protests was rated almost certain, and it came true and then some. The turnout of 575,000 to 600,000 exceeded the forecast of 'several hundred thousand,' and the movement broadened beyond students to include trade unions and nationwide strikes, which was not explicitly predicted. The government's response was a step more substantive than the expected 'small concessions': bringing forward a minimum wage hike and announcing a social conference. The expectation that grievances over cost of living and student funding would remain unresolved was confirmed, as the budget was unanimously rejected by parliament, deepening rather than resolving the impasse.

The market and fiscal reaction to Fitch was rated probable and came true in a different, sharper form. Rather than a mid-term budget revision or a pledge of spending cuts, the parliament simply rejected the budget outright, and the Bank of France is expected to cut its 2026 GDP forecast. The expectation that the government would lean on rhetoric rather than immediate action was broadly correct, but the rejection of the budget was a more dramatic event than the gradual yield volatility that was anticipated.

The Le Pen campaign momentum was rated probable and came true, but the story expanded well beyond Le Pen. The expectation of at least one major rally or media appearance was met, but the bigger development was the widening of the field: Teddy Riner's presidential announcement was a complete surprise not on the expectation list, and Mélenchon's call to exit NATO and Macron's failed coalition proposal added layers of political chaos that were not anticipated. The rising odds of a Le Pen-Mélenchon runoff, noted by Reuters in the first photograph, were reinforced by the polls showing both ahead.

The Trappes shooting case was rated possible for developing further, and it was the expectation that most clearly did not come. The suspect's psychiatric evaluation, a possible pre-trial hearing, and continued public mourning were all anticipated, but by the second photograph the case had largely faded from the headlines. No major procedural step was reported. This suggests the case, while emotionally powerful, lacked the institutional momentum to sustain a news cycle against the backdrop of larger political and economic events.

The government political response was rated possible and came true in a mixed form. The budget rejection and the minimum wage concession fit the expectation of the government trying to show it is in control. However, the 'Rioters Pay' bill, which was expected to move through its legislative process, did not appear prominently in the second photograph, suggesting it was either shelved or overshadowed. The expectation of a parliamentary question period or special session was broadly met by the budget vote.

The ECB and Eurozone follow-up was rated possible and was the weakest of the expectations. The ECB commentary and European Commission reaction on France's fiscal trajectory were anticipated, but the second photograph shows the domestic budget rejection as the dominant fiscal story, with the ECB playing a quieter role. The 42-million-barrel oil release was not a prominent follow-up.

Sports and culture were rated possible and came true, though the specific events shifted. The expectation of PSG playing in Ligue 1 and the Mbappé situation being a talking point were met. The Rugby Nations Championship and Alcaraz's Paris Masters victory were not specifically predicted but fit the general expectation of sports generating coverage. The Olympics leadership change, which was a notable story in the first photograph, faded as expected.

Among the less likely surprises, the major concession package (minimum wage hike brought forward, social conference) came true, which was only rated possible. The second wave of cyberattacks also came true and in a much more dramatic form than the 'unlikely but possible' rating suggested: the Iran blame, the blood bank hit, and the 100 million euro loss at Credit Mutuel Arkea turned a minor note into a top story. A government reshuffle or ministerial resignation was not clearly seen. A snap parliamentary dissolution did not happen.

Among the things we would not bet on, a full-scale general strike did not quite materialise, though the nationwide SNCF strike and union participation came close. A major new terrorist attack did not occur. A full fiscal consolidation plan was not announced, consistent with the expectation. A Le Pen-Mélenchon debate did not happen. A sudden ceasefire with a grand bargain did not occur.

The overall pattern of misses suggests the expectation framework underestimated two things: the speed at which the protest movement would broaden beyond students to include unions and the Yellow Vests, and the potential for the cyberattack story to escalate into a diplomatic and financial crisis. The framework also overestimated the staying power of the Trappes shooting as a standalone news cycle and underestimated the political chaos that would emerge from the widening 2027 candidate field. The G7 meeting in Paris was an entirely unanticipated event that added a diplomatic dimension to the week.
delta.driver: The force pushing France from the first photograph to the second is the collision of a generational cost-of-living crisis with a political class that cannot agree on how to pay for it. The protests are not a single event but a pressure valve: students, workers, and now the Yellow Vests are all saying the same thing in different registers, that wages have not kept up with prices and the state is not managing the fiscal transition fairly. The unanimous rejection of the budget by parliament is the political expression of that same impasse, a legislature that cannot agree on spending while the government cannot cut it. Into this domestic stalemate, two external shocks landed in the same week: the Iran cyberattack, which turned a technical incident into a question of national security and sovereignty, and the G7 meeting in Paris, which forced France to host and project stability while its own streets were on fire. The widening of the 2027 presidential field, with Riner, Mélenchon's NATO exit call, and Macron's failed coalition, shows that no political camp can yet claim the centre, and the centrist fragmentation that was a background story in the first photograph has become the main story. What is driving this country, in short, is the gap between a population that feels economically left behind and a political system that is too divided, too slow, and too focused on the 2027 race to close that gap quickly enough.

crystal.headline: France's Fifth Weekend of Riots Collides With Iran Cyber Retaliation
emoji_reasons: Five consecutive weekends of mass protests, now with unions, Yellow Vests, and a 'mass disobedience' call, make this the dominant and most consequential story of the week.

France's official blame of Iran for the supermarket, blood-bank, and banking cyberattacks, its vow of retaliation, and the 100-million-euro loss at Credit Mutuel Arkea turn a technical incident into a diplomatic and financial crisis.

The unanimous budget rejection, the likely Bank of France GDP forecast cut, Fitch's negative outlook, and the need for a parliamentary response make the fiscal impasse the structural undercurrent beneath every other story.
crystal.tldr: France enters its fifth consecutive weekend of mass protests, likely larger and more radical than the last, as the government struggles to turn its social-conference promise into concrete policy while parliament remains deadlocked over the budget. The Iran cyberattack story escalates into a diplomatic and financial confrontation, with France expected to announce a specific retaliation and Iran to respond. The 2027 presidential field widens further with Riner's first campaign moves and Mélenchon's NATO-exit debate, while the Rugby Nations Championship reaches its decisive France-South Africa match at Twickenham.
crystal.eli5:
France is in the middle of a really big argument about money. For five Saturdays in a row, hundreds of thousands of people have marched in the streets, and now the unions and the Yellow Vests have joined in. The government tried to calm things down by promising higher minimum wages and a big meeting to talk about fairness, but parliament just voted down the government's budget, which means nobody can agree on how to pay for the things people want. This week, the protests will probably happen again, maybe even bigger, and the government will have to show it is actually doing something, not just talking.

At the same time, someone hacked into French supermarket refrigerators, blood banks, and a big bank, and France says it was Iran. France lost about 100 million euros at one bank, and now it says it is going to hit back. Iran is going to argue back. This is turning into a small cold war over computers, and the US is watching and probably helping.

On top of all that, everyone is already talking about the 2027 presidential election. A judo champion just said he wants to run, the left is saying France should leave NATO, and the center is arguing with itself. And on Saturday, the French rugby team plays South Africa in a really important match, but their best playmaker is injured, so it is a tough one. It is a very loud, very busy week in France.

judgment.comparison: Both forecasts correctly identified the week's dominant story (fourth weekend of protests, even larger than expected at 575,000-600,000), the fiscal pressure (Fitch, budget rejection, GDP forecast cut), Le Pen's campaign momentum, and the government's struggle to respond. Both correctly ruled out a general strike, a state of emergency, a snap election, and a full fiscal consolidation plan. Both missed the G7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris and Teddy Riner's presidential announcement. Both underweighted the cyberattack escalation, though B at least treated it as a live thread while A filed it under 'less likely surprises.' B's economic section is more nuanced and accurate, capturing the 'riot premium,' the specific corporate stress events (Credit Mutuel Arkea, SocGen), and the finance minister's market-facing communication. A's sports section is more specific and hits more targets (PSG, Mbappé, 2030 Olympics), while B is vaguer on sports. A's structure is cleaner with explicit confidence levels, but B's extra detail came true more often. For a reader trying to understand what the coming week would look like, B provides a richer and more accurate picture of the political, economic, and social dynamics, while A is a competent but thinner overview.
